$comment: Sidecar metadata for the composite pipe lesson (S04 variant composite.contraction-run). Codes and short paraphrased labels only. NCSE 2026 codes supplied by the product owner in Run 2B, not fetched from the standard. Nothing here is verified or reviewed.

specFCodes: F3 + F4 (S08: Colebrook law with a bisection root finder)
fidelity.modelForm: algebraic mechanical-energy balance with lumped contraction loss and Darcy–Weisbach friction
fidelity.solutionMethod: closed form, plus bracketed bisection for Colebrook
fidelity.dataDependency: empirical Colebrook law (historical roughened-pipe data); user-supplied K; editable constant fluid properties

tasks.title: Level contraction at fixed flow
tasks.evidenceType: numeric prediction of v₂ and p₂ − p₁ committed before reveal; comparison with the ideal (Bernoulli) prediction; answers to items A1–A3; short explanation

fields.label: Your predicted mean velocity just after the contraction, v̄₂
Your predicted change in static pressure p₂ − p₁ (negative if it falls)

items.stem: At fixed Q the bore halves from 50 mm to 25 mm. The ratio v̄₂/v̄₁ is:

options.feedback: Velocity scales with 1/area, and area scales with D², so halving D quarters the area.
Correct. Continuity at fixed Q gives v = Q/A with A = πD²/4, so v₂/v₁ = (D₁/D₂)² = 4.
This inverts the effect. The same volume per second passes through a smaller area, so it must move faster.
Equal velocities would need equal areas. Only the mass flow ṁ is the same at both stations.

items.stem: In the ideal level contraction, the static pressure at station 2 compared with station 1 is:

options.feedback: Correct. Total head is conserved in the ideal model; the velocity head rises by (v₂² − v₁²)/2g, so the pressure head must fall by the same amount (z unchanged).
A common intuition is that squeezing the flow raises pressure. In steady flow the fluid accelerates into the narrow section, and that needs a pressure fall in the flow direction.
The pressure would stay the same only if the velocity head did not change, which needs equal areas.

items.stem: Using the ideal prediction, enter p₁ − p₂ in Pa (within 1%).
items.feedbackCorrect: Correct: p₁ − p₂ = ρ(v₂² − v₁²)/2 for a level ideal contraction.
items.feedbackIncorrect: Use p₁ − p₂ = ρ(v₂² − v₁²)/2 with v from continuity. Check that you squared the velocities and used ρ in kg/m³.

tasks.title: Ideal and lossy predictions for the same pipe
tasks.evidenceType: numeric prediction of the head difference between ideal and lossy p₃ committed before reveal; head-budget accounting; answers to items B1–B3; short explanation

fields.label: Your predicted head difference (p₃ ideal − p₃ lossy)/(ρg)
Which loss do you expect to be larger?

illustrativeValues.note: Illustrative teaching value chosen by the author, not from a correlation; needs SME confirmation (OPEN_QUESTIONS OQ-05).

items.stem: The ideal p₃ exceeds the lossy p₃ by:

options.feedback: Correct. Both predictions share p₁, v and z; the only difference is the dissipated head h_K + h_f, which appears as pressure at the same elevation and velocity.
The contraction loss h_K = K v₂²/2g is also dissipated, so it lowers p₂ and therefore p₃.
The velocity head is the same in both predictions (same Q and D₂), so it cannot explain the difference.

options.text: Nothing: losses only affect the velocity
options.feedback: In steady flow at fixed Q the velocity is set by continuity. Losses reduce pressure, not velocity.

items.stem: Between stations 1 and 3, which change in head could in principle be recovered by changing the downstream geometry?

options.text: The rise in velocity head (for example with a diffuser)
options.feedback: Correct. Kinetic energy is a conversion of pressure head and can be partly converted back; dissipated head cannot.
Wall friction dissipates mechanical energy as heat; it is not recoverable as pressure.
h_K is a dissipation (eddies and mixing) lumped into K. It is lost, not stored.

items.stem: Enter the total dissipated head H₁ − H₃ in m (within 2%).
items.feedbackCorrect: Correct: H₁ − H₃ = h_K + h_f, the length of the loss bar.
items.feedbackIncorrect: Add h_K = K v₂²/2g and h_f = f (L/D₂) v₂²/2g, or read the two dissipated segments of the head-budget bar.

tasks.title: Push the model to an applicability limit
tasks.evidenceType: numeric prediction of the flow at Re₂ = 4000 committed before exploring; record of the limit reached; answers to items C1–C3; explanation of the extra model, correlation or data needed

eaStage1.label: Limits of current knowledge and models

ncse2026.label: Bounds of safe and sustainable practice

fields.label: Your predicted flow at which Re₂ falls to 4000

items.stem: When Re₂ is between 2300 and 4000 the lesson shows Re but no friction factor or friction pressure drop. Why?

options.text: No friction model in scope is valid there: the thresholds are conventions, and transition depends on disturbances the model does not know
options.feedback: Correct. Withholding a number is the honest output when no validated model covers the state.

options.text: The flow stops in the transition band
options.feedback: Q and v are unchanged; the fluid still flows. Only the friction prediction is withdrawn.

options.text: The Colebrook equation has no solution there
options.feedback: Colebrook can be solved numerically at Re = 3000, but its stated basis is fully turbulent flow; a solution is not the same as validity.
Friction does not vanish in transition; it is simply not predicted reliably by either branch.

items.stem: What would let you predict the pressure drop for this pipe in the transition band?

options.text: Measured Δp against Q on this pipe, with calibration, uncertainty and the flow conditions recorded
options.feedback: Correct. Measured data for the actual geometry and disturbance level is the defensible basis; a transition correlation would need evidence for this geometry too.
64/Re is the laminar, fully developed result; using it above 2300 extrapolates outside its domain.

options.text: Average the laminar and turbulent friction factors
options.feedback: Interpolating across the transition gap is explicitly prohibited by the applicability standard: it has no physical basis.
Numerical accuracy cannot fix model-form uncertainty.

items.stem: For the current D₂ and fluid, enter the flow at which Re₂ = 4000, in L/min (within 2%).
items.feedbackCorrect: Correct: Q = Re π D₂ μ /(4ρ).
items.feedbackIncorrect: Rearrange Re₂ = 4ρQ/(π D₂ μ) for Q, then convert m³/s to L/min (× 60 000).

equations.text: p₂ = p₁ + ρ(v₁² − v₂²)/2 − ρg h_K;  p₃ = p₂ − ρg z₃ − ρg h_f
